utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, April Carter, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Colonel Tucker, I know you know it but I must remind you, you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith, before you start, just to remind the parties that we are probably going to sit for one and a half sessions today, we don't have interpreters. And if you are able to indicate how long you are going to be so that maybe the Registrar might start arranging for recalling Colonel Tucker or postponing to a date where Colonel Tucker could be able to attend, otherwise, Mr. Saxon, you may have to recall him, if we don't finish with him. Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you like me to address that question first, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you are able to very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very briefly, I hope to be, if things go as planned, I hope to be done within a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I have no idea what the redirect is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two subject matters to address with the colonel, so it should be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, with the notion of time for the moment not being our friend, I'm going to move to another subject quickly in an attempt to expedite matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have 1D02-5508 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Something is funny here, I don't hear you through my earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you hear me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you like that but not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You don't hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes? Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was 1D02-5508.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm going to do right now is I'm going to show you a series of documents, most of which cover matters that we have discussed already, and I'd like you to take a look at them briefly, if you could, and then see whether or not these are documents that are familiar to you and the information contained therein is information of which you know. Okay? The first document obviously, as you can tell is an UNMO briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next -- dated 16th November, 1993. Could we turn to the next page. Just go to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, as I understand, this would be at a time when you were no longer in the region; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So this is not a document that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the type of document I'm familiar with, but this one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could now have up on the screen, please, 1D02-5778.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next document I'm going to show you is from the headquarters of United Kingdom land forces. It's -- the date is the 10th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the first paragraph which is 1(a).

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if you -- can you read that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that indicates that: "The Muslim counter-offensive in response to the fall of Cerska continues but without marked success." Is this information that you reported?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is information which was reported by the British battalion which had forces -- or had troops up in the Tuzla pocket, if I remember they were commanded by a major Abrahams and his unit was reporting both to United Nations in other words to Kiseljak but was also sending independent UK national reports to the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. And turning to the next page which is page 2, paragraph (b). I believe you at one point mentioned the name of a gentleman, Mr. Hollingsworth?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It hasn't come up yet, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's page 3. There we go. Great. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Paragraph (b) states: "Mr. Larry Hollingsworth on return from the Cerska area confirmed that the situation is not as black as previously painted. There are no overt signs of a massacre, no obvious cases of malnutrition and some fuel is available." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is consistent with -- Larry Hollingsworth was with General Morillon when he went to Cerska, and this is what we covered yesterday. This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, could I have that marked as the Defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit D00190.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Next, if I could have, please, 1D02-6051.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you are not tendering the first document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I'm not because the witness has no familiarity with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe this is a document that you -- that you penned or drafted?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this, I believe, among other things refers to a different mortar attack than the mortar attacks that we've been previously discussing with regard to the Bosniak Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2. And if we could go to the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before I ask you any questions with regard to the information that is contained in paragraph 2, Colonel Siber, he was a member of the which army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Siber was a member of the Presidency army, in other words, the ABiH. However, he was ethnically a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And I thank you for that answer because, I think, yesterday there may be some confusion with regard to his exact status, so. In paragraph 2, there is a discussion concerning a mortar attack on FRBAT2. Would that be FrenchBat 2?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I understand what occurred is that there was a fatality or fatalities suffered as a result of a mortar attack by the Presidency on an UNPROFOR unit, that being FrenchBat 2; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were casualties. I can't remember the exact details of how many, and from the crater analysis carried out by a Canadian officer, Major Itani [phoen], he was able to determine that those shells had not been fired from -- or appeared as they had not been fired by the Bosnian Serb side but by the ABiH side or from ABiH territory, to be absolutely precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that paragraph there are a couple of noteworthy features, which is, one, that there was apparently an argument about how you can determine the direction from which a shell came by crater analysis; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And based upon your conversation with Colonel Siber at least as late as February 1993, it would appear, and I'm using your words here, it would appear that the BH Army is not aware of techniques of crater analysis. That's what you state there, correct, sir? That's what you state there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also -- continuing in this paragraph, Colonel Siber says there were unruly elements in and attached to the BH Army. Now, I take it by that there was some discussion about whether or not he had control over those individuals who may well have been responsible for this attack, although there was not any specific identification of who those individuals were; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Also on -- turning to page 2 now, there's also an indication -- oh, I shouldn't say -- I should say an indication as well as a reporting of a BH Army infantry attack on Ilidza from Butmir and Stup. And that's in paragraph (b) once it gets up on the screen. And that's going to be right below the chart. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That there was an attack on the 11th of February by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, sat here today, recall specific details, but if that's what I wrote at the time, I did write that report, then that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Turning now to, I believe it will be the fifth page. It will be the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this is referring once again to that same fatal mortar attack; correct? This is the report --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- in a different form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Turning now to the seventh page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is the letter that was written -- I take it this is the letter that you drafted on behalf of General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in this letter it's indicated in paragraph 1 that: "It is sadly beyond doubt that your forces were responsible." Correct? That's what you stated?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Which is slightly different from what you told us but a moment a ago, when you had done an investigation and determination had been made at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the difference was that that was a single determination, a single instant, this is talking about a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. This here is talking about a pattern of behaviour? I see, okay. And finally the last page which is also dated the 13th of February, this letter deals with a slightly different issue. Yesterday, as you recall, we were talking about the independent and unilateral decision of the UNHCR to not supply humanitarian aid. In this situation what occurred, as I understand it from the letter, is that at some point the Presidency made a determination that they were going refuse humanitarian aid, and this caused some distress to General Morillon, or that's what this letter states; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The Presidency declared they were going to refuse to receive humanitarian -- accept humanitarian aid elsewhere in Bosnia in solidarity with the eastern enclaves who were not receiving aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And elsewhere in Bosnia obviously including Sarajevo, which is --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have that document marked as Defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit D191. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to have up on the screen if I could is 1D02-6044, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document is dated the 26th, and it concerns a series -- in its subject matter of discussions with Mladic, and it's from an individual by the name of Wahlgren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it the 26th or 29th?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have the 26th, Your Honour, as the subject discussions with Mladic -- I'm sorry, I understand your question. The document is dated the 29th, it refers to conversations had with Mladic on the 26th of March, 1993. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it's from a gentleman by the name of Wahlgren. First of all, do you know who Wahlgren is?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of UNPROFOR in Zagreb and he took over from General Nambiar who was his predecessor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So then in terms of the -- in terms of the chain of command then, he would have been above General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon reported to General Wahlgren.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. With regard to this particular document --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm just going to ask is whether or not this is a document that you are familiar with, first of all?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with the document because it was sent from Zagreb to the United Nations, and I was in Belgrade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn now to, then, page 4 of 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's a section here that says: "Mladic says he wants peace but there were some requirements that must be met." He discusses the withdrawal of the Croatian forces which seems to have been a relatively consistent theme from the time that you very -- you had your first encounter or meeting with him; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to skip B for the moment and go on to the next paragraph, which says: "He requested," that would be once again Mladic, "that a cease-fire be organised by the coming together of military chiefs of all four parties and suggested that in the interest of peace in the future, that they all stick to it. He said that he had declared ..." That would be Mladic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "... a cease-fire in 29 December 1992 and there was no response." Are you aware, first of all, of this conversation with Wahlgren?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- this is a document which looks as if it's a report about the meeting with Mladic that I described yesterday. I was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is the information that's contained in what I just read accurate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge and understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph, it says: "He ..." Once again that would be Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "... indicated UNPROFOR can count on his full support and cooperation. He reiterated that it was a pity that we did not do what we had discussed on the 3 March 1993 (Morillon and Mladic)."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I would have to look in my notes. I can't recall because whenever Morillon met with Mladic, there were 10, 15 issues that they discussed. And I would have to look in my notes in order to find out what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to hold on that just because I'm pushing through as quickly as I can; we'll try to get back to that one issue if we can. All right? It goes on to say: "He said that he was ready to let the Muslims go, if they so wish, to Tuzla and he expected a reciprocal arrangement for the Serbs of Tuzla. He is prepared to talk about the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina issue, despite the fact that the earlier cease-fire had been violated. The following being his initiatives." Then he goes on with the initiatives onto the next page. And then the report, after we talk about his initiatives, A, which -- A or A, B, C and D, then there is a report of those agreements that were attempted to be obtained from him. Right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, at this point in time - and by this point in time, I mean March 26 of 1993 - a report had been made - had it not? - to the United Nations Security Council with regard to the interim arrangements, do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have D155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the fate of this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to move its admission. I will move its admission. If we could have that marked as the Defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D192. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document which has previously been admitted in evidence is the report of the Secretary-General on the activities of The International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia peace talks on Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the reference of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's Defendant's 155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is a document that discusses the efforts and arrangements that have been made for a comprehensive peace concerning pretty much everything that could be envisioned by the co-chairman. Are you aware of the fact that there had been a myriad meetings between pretty much the time that you first arrived, if not before, in Bosnia, certainly up to and including this report with regard to a comprehensive peace plan that took into account such things as geographic boundaries, the manner in which fuel, electricity would be regulated, the form of government, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that, and I've met with Vance and Owen and a number of others involved in those negotiations because they would come to Sarajevo from time to time to meet with General Morillon and with members of the Presidency and Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of what would be the geographic boundaries, was a map presented to all the parties and reported to the United Nations Security Council with regard to how, I hate to use the word, but how this region would be broken up or divided?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally see or hand over any maps, but I know maps were being worked on. And that I know that -- that Lord Owen certainly was involved with some maps, but I did not personally see those maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure, and I'll have to double-check, give me but a second. I'm just double-checking because it's a relatively long document; I want to give you the proper page in e-court that we should be pulling up. Perfect, the system does work. If we could please have page 24 in e-court of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to this map, does this map comport with the map that you claim to have seen when you spoke with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this map looks totally different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the map that you -- I'm -- the map that you claim to have seen and discussed with Dr. Karadzic, is that a map that -- that you reported about? Did you make a report about that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I referred to it in one or two sentences, but did not make a specific report. It was the rest of the meeting which was the main subject of the reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to make sure about something before I go any further, because I want to make sure that what I have seen of your notes is an accurate reflection of what you turned over to the Prosecution. So I ask you the following question which is: Are all the notes that you brought with you that were the subject matter of some discussion a couple of days ago, the self-same notes that you turned over to the Prosecution? There's nothing new in those notes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One comment I would make is that those notes are not every single page of notes I made while I was in Bosnia, there were some short periods of when I didn't have that note or those notebooks with me, and those notes I no longer have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to -- with regard to the issue that I'm referring to right now which is this meeting that you had with Dr. Karadzic in which you claim that there was this discussion about a very specific map, which has been specifically identified, that was a pretty important piece of information, was it not? It's the kind of piece of information that would be indicative of what the intent of parties were and how one was to negotiate and what kinds of expectations could be seen with regard to, among other things, your mandate; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In hindsight, you are correct. At that time this map was brought out - I'm referring to the census map - was brought out by Karadzic and General Mladic effectively during the coffee break in between the meeting. And one of the things that happened in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, you're well past my question. You said in hindsight it was, but I take it at the time it was not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And this map is a map that you referred to in the testimony that you have given previously?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. So just so we are clear for purposes of the record, a document which you've specifically identified there are no notes of, you have testified at least thrice in these proceedings and you have never raised this issue before; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I was not asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that you were not -- I understand that that's a kind of stock response here when dealing with matters that are somewhat critical, but that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Mr. Guy-Smith be prohibitive from being argumentative with the witness in regards to the "stock" answers and allegations against this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please do make sure that you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the second map that you claim to have seen, the Vinko map, I take it that we have the same situation? There are no notes, and you've never testified about it before?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unclear of what you mean by Vinko map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies. Pandurevic map. The map that you --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh right. No, of course not. That was a map which was in his headquarters on his wall and which I only saw for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And so you saw the map and as you've told us here because these are two things that have featured prominently in your testimony here before us, you saw the map for about five minutes; there are no notes that you took with regard to the map; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You made -- you didn't make a report to anybody concerning the map, which is as a matter of fact, excuse me, which as a matter of fact is relatively critical as regards what is occurring specifically in terms of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pandurevic map, I did report and we did report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. When?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- I can't, sat here now today, say when, but in the next report that I was sending from the -- from that area. If you recall, I said yesterday that we were regularly radioing in reports. And in one of those reports that would have been included.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another topic, which is you indicated that there was a convoy of humanitarian aid that was stuck, that had come from Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which convoys are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The one that was on the -- I believe it was stuck at the Zvornik bridge.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the convoys which came from -- which were stuck at the Zvornik bridge always came from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. So we are clear, humanitarian aid that had been determined was necessary for this area was emanating from Belgrade, and by that I mean geographically came from that region, and it was stuck, meaning that the Bosnian Serbs, for whatever their reasons may be, refused to let it pass?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know who it came from in the Belgrade region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was flown into Belgrade airport and UNHCR had a big depo at Belgrade airport which at that time was under sanction. So it was -- the UN traffic was virtually the only traffic through the airport. And it was then trucked from Belgrade airport down to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm trying to be efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let us return now to Morillon after he has come back from Cerska at which point he has a conversation with Oric, and once again to set the stage, he had been told by Oric of the horrors that we discussed yesterday including many wounded and people being put in houses and burned, and he came back and spoke to Oric about this and said to Oric --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just clarify? Are you talking about when General Morillon spoke with Oric in Konjevic Polje literally hours after he came back from Cerska, or do you mean when he spoke with Oric in Srebrenica about eight or ten days later?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe I'm referring to the first conversation.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in Konjevic Polje literally a couple of hours after he had been in -- yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that conversation he indicated to Commander Oric that he had been in the area, he had seen what he had seen, and that the reports that were made were grossly exaggerated, if not in some senses false; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Oric -- Oric's reply, as least as I understand it from prior testimony, was he shrugged his shoulders and said, Well, I heard it from a bunch of my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I never checked it out.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't able to go into Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was pretty much the end that have as far as he was concerned?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Allegation was made, turned out not to be true, no big deal; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, same conversation was also had with President Izetbegovic and I believe Mr. Ganic at a later point in time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about a day later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And once again, the same information was conveyed to Izetbegovic and to Ganic that the information that had been relayed, the information that in many senses was the causative factor for you marshalling the helicopters and going into the region turned out to be not only not accurate, but in certain regards palpably false; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the way you describe it, yes, but had there been heavy fighting? Had there been casualties caused? Yes there were. Were there people that were starving? Yes there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's not the issue, my friend, and we both well know it. The issue is the question of burned bodies and the horrors of the falling of Cerska and the need for immediate intervention because of the horrors that had been occasioned in the area by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, on that specific you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am correct.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So did President Izetbegovic take the same kind of position that Commander Oric took which was, you know, I got the information from other people but I never checked it out?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic thanked General Morillon for going in and for confirming that there had not been this massacre. However, that it looked as if the crisis was unfolding in Srebrenica and asked General Morillon to go back to Srebrenica, which is where General Morillon also reported that whilst there had been reports of 700 injured in Konjevic Polje and that he only found 73, or rather Dr. Mardell only found 73 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are not answering my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. My question was: "So did President Izetbegovic take the same kind of position that Commander Oric took which was, I got the information from other people but I never checked it out?" And I'm referring to to that specific issue.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is you who added the context, but I never checked it out. The issue is that President Izetbegovic was surrounded in Sarajevo and was in no position to go and do any checking out. As you somewhat facilely put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you in other terms then, sir. Did he indicate to you after he was told that the information that he received was inaccurate and in some regards palpably false, what he had done in order to determine the accuracy of the information that he was giving to you upon which he was asking you to operate? Did he say who he had talked to, what had been done, how can we stop this from happening again? Because as we both know, and it's an old saw, truth is one of the casualties, not necessarily first, but one of the casualties of war. So did he discuss that matter with you? So how to fix this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this being a compound question and more so a compound speech. And I would ask that the witness to be asked a single question at a time and being allowed to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did he, President Izetbegovic, indicate that he was concerned to you about the fact that you had received incorrect and palpably false information with regard to what was occurring in Cerska, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did he, President Izetbegovic, discuss with you a way, a mechanism whereby wild rumours could be avoided with regard to such things as war crimes and humanitarian crises as exemplified with Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you for a moment, if I could, about what I think is fairly characterised as the night-attempted escapes from Sarajevo through the airport. You know the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there are daily sitrep reports with regard to this issue, which I think we are both aware of. But time is not our friend right here, so I'm going to try to summarise what I understand was occurring. In the night-time, hundreds of people on a nightly basis were attempting to leave Sarajevo through the airport area; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In the winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, in the winter. The majority of those people were men; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot testify to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When I say hundreds, would you agree with me, and I'm trying to be conservative here, that what was occurring was there was a report of approximately 300 to 400 people a night attempting to leave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes it was more, sometimes it was less.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm trying to average it out. And what happened was that they were stopped by the UNPROFOR unit at the airport, and I'm not sure if they were either arrested or just turned back; do you know?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were rounded up and taken back to where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There came a point in time where this became a sufficient enough problem that it was decided that it would no longer be reported about; correct? The reporting was stopped?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but one of the main reasons reporting was stopped was not simple because of the numbers but because of the numbers who were being shot by Bosnian Serb snipers whilst they were trying to run across the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, with regard to the general situation and assessment --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have 1D02-6159 which you will have as probably pages 1 and 2 of 1D02-6025. What occurred here is there were -- it doesn't matter what occurred, I'm sure that Mr. Registrar will be able to get to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you are looking for that, can I just ask something for clarification. Are you saying the reason you stopped reporting about this is because numbers were being shot by Bosnian Serb snipers while they were trying to run across the airport? Wasn't that kind of incident precisely the kind of thing that you were supposed to be reporting, where people are being sniped at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was concern -- I don't recollect immediately sat here, I'd need to go back into notes, what the specific logic was. It was concern that people were trying to escape out of Sarajevo and escape from the conditions and that people were being shot whilst trying to escape. French soldiers were being shot at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my question is, if you say you stopped reporting because they were being sniped at, my question is: Was the question of sniping not the very thing that you ought to be looking out for and reporting and trying to avoid to the extent possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with you, sir. But nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But nonetheless you stopped reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would we call that dereliction of duty?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was uncomfortable with it at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. If we could have the next page, please. Page 2. Go down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The bottom the page is an assessment which I think is discussing the matter that we've been dealing with: "Assessment: The nightly airport crossings are becoming an increasing problem. Larger numbers of people (now mostly men) are crossing. Dense fog and a new tactic of crossing in larger groups result in more people slipping past FREBAT soldiers who are being overwhelmed. The danger is that as more men slip from one side to the other, the Serbs may decide that UNPROFOR is unable to stop the flow of potential fighters and intervene with fire, placing UN troops at risk and escalating the conflict. As well, FREBAT finds its soldiers working day (escorting aid, et cetera) and night (stopping crossings), a negotiated settlement is essential although this seems unlikely. A separate report will be sent on this critical situation." Is that a fair --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair encapsulation of the problem and the situation that we are referring to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And goes some way to not giving full answers, but partial answers to your earlier question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to focus for a moment on what I understood your testimony to be with regard to what you were doing and why you were doing it, okay? And I'd like to refer you to something that you've previously said and see whether or not this is consistent with what you've been talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm referring Court and counsel to IT-03-68 pages 5838 and 5839.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked the following question by a representative of the Prosecution: "Thank you. Now, you have given evidence of some of the objective of your trip." And this is your trip to Srebrenica. "Were they the principal objectives, namely, facilitation of the aid convoy, facilitation of cease-fires, deployment of UNMOs or military observers, and evacuation of the injured. Is that a --" And your answer is: "Those are the four objectives, though I put them in a different order. I would put them in the order of ..." And one, the first point is: "Deploy UNMOs first because you need them to have a cease-fire, and you needed the cease-fire in order to get the humanitarian aid through in order to evacuate the injured."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And as a matter of fact, if I'm not mistaken, when you first began your conversations with Bosnian Serb representatives, and specifically with Mladic, the issue that was at hand was the issue of a cease-fire, the cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in all of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have made it much easier to get humanitarian aid through to where it was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed so. I told you that we would get back to the issue of demilitarisation yesterday, and I would like to deal with demilitarisation with you now. When you were in Srebrenica in March, this would be of 1993, you had discussions with both the war committee of Srebrenica and Commander Oric cap? Concerning demilitarisation, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before we discuss what those were, who or what was the war committee of Srebrenica, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it was the mayor of Srebrenica and a number of other councillors, whether they are elected or not, I have no idea. There was also a doctor from the Srebrenica hospital, and there were a couple of military people. However, they were not Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The subject matter of demilitarisation was something that was important for purposes of seeing what could be done in obtaining a cease-fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the angles in to how you would achieve a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because obviously if an area is demilitarised, there's no fighting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The war committee, after some discussion, I believe, agreed to demilitarise Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm talking about during the period of time you were there. They were inclined, perhaps I've been too strong, they were inclined to demilitarise while you were there in your discussions with them?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- to the best of my recollection, it was something they were considering; Morillon had asked them. But by the time that -- at the time that I left, I don't think a decision had been made on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oric was vehemently opposed to demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what Oric's position was was that there would be no demilitarisation and he would fight to the last man standing; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he used those words, but that's what it boiled down to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the time that that issue was being discussed, to your knowledge was Oric involved in either offensive actions or raids against the --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of specific raids or actions, but when Morillon asked Oric were his people still carrying out attacks in general, Oric said, Yes, they were. How do you think I'm getting -- we are getting the ammunition and weapons with which to defend ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact what was occurring is that the Bosnian Serbs were using the Oric attacks and/or raids, however you wish to call them, as a basis for continuing their efforts against Srebrenica? I'm not saying -- you know, that's what was going on. I'm not putting any value on it, but that's what was being said to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was going on and went on in Bosnia all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact you were told by the Bosnian Serbs that Oric and his men were massacring and killing civilians, and that would be Serb civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the Bosnian Serbs said is that civilians had been massacred in January, we've already covered some of that ground. At this time, in other words, in March when we were in Srebrenica, the Bosnian Serbs said that, if I remember, between 7 and 15 people were being killed every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that -- when you had a discussion with Oric about this, Oric said that, and I don't know if these were exact words, but something to the effect of, you know, Perhaps my men are a bit vengeful, so when it's only necessary to kill one, we kill two, two for one?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he acknowledged that that was not the best thing in the world but he didn't know whether or not he could get his troops to stop engaging in that kind of behaviour; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the other side of this there was a meeting, and I think this is around the time of March 15th, there was a discussion in which Morillon was to have said that, I believe you noted this. "I know you wish to clean out this nest of terrorists. I will do it for you and save you many, many casualties." Now, all I care about for the moment, is that something that Morillon said to Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sat here now today, I recollect something along those lines, whether the words "this nest of terrorists" were used specifically, I can't remember. But what I do remember was that what Morillon was appealing to was, Stop attacking them; I will try and stop them attacking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I can be of some help to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring Court and counsel to page 5984 IT-03-68 in which you were asked the following question and you give the following answers. Now, if we go a bit further down you have line 16 to 18: "I know you wish to clean out this nest of terrorists, I will do it for you and save you many many casualties. "A. Yes. "Q. That's General Morillon speaking to the Serbs and referring to Srebrenica as the nest of terrorists; is that correct? "A. He was speaking in language the Serbs would understand. That was the language which the Serbs had been using for General Morillon to refer to them, otherwise it would have been difficult in the circumstances." So you give an explanation of why he used that language; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is something that he said? And I'm just talking about the bald words that were used.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whatever interpretation we put on them is something entirely different, but those were the bald words that he used?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have but a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I tried to make good my promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Madam Carter, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, today you were asked about the maps in both Karadzic's office as well as in Pandurevic's office and when you actually reported those items.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to now bring up 1D02-5546.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecution beginning on 6 and 7 September and then later carrying on both in 2001 and 2002?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to move to page 23 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in the middle of the page we began a conversation in regard to Srebrenica in March of 1993. At that time you told the Office of the Prosecution that: "I later learned that this offensive had been launched on 7 February when Morillon and I happened to be in the office of major Pandurevic, in a Bosnian Serb army barracks just outside of Zvornik. Pandurevic had maps on his wall that detailed the Bosnian Serb Army's advance on the eastern enclaves, and these had dates and lines on them which showed how far the advance had progressed." Are these the one in the same maps that you testified to in court these past days?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to Exhibit D192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to D192, what would you like to happen to ID02-5546?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't need to tender this in evidence. I merely wanted to point out to -- or make a clarification of the record that the veiled allegations of fabrication were unfounded and that he had in fact reported not only to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, yes, I believe that as a matter of fact, the redirect as posed did not deal with the specific question asked which was, Was there reportage of it? Which is different than having a conversation with the Prosecution about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess, yeah, that's a question of argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Obviously it's a question for your -- obviously that's a question for your determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, as I say, it's a question for argument. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you asked for D192.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you were questioned on the meeting of 26 March 1993 and this report on 29 March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to page 5 of this report. At the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of your meeting with Mladic, there's an indication that there was a meeting with General Panic which followed. Can you please tell us who General Panic is?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Panic, my understanding, was the Chief of Staff of the Serb military in Belgrade. In other words, of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Turning to the following page, there's an indication that the meeting actually involved both Panic and Mladic at the same time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, sir, this report is indicating that Panic stated that the warring parties in BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina, should be separated on the lines of which they now stand; is that correct? It's in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't specifically remember, sat here now today, of what was specifically said at that meeting 17 years ago. However, it is consistent with everything else that -- that was being said again and again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And being said by whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being said by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. What about the Belgrade Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot specifically remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I want to turn to some of the examination from yesterday in which you were discussing with Mr. Guy-Smith the cessation or suspension of the UNHCR convoys into Srebrenica on or about 17 November 1992. At that time you were being questioned, you indicated that the circumstances were a bit more complicated than what was being asked of you in court today. Can you please tell me, what was complicating the situations in regards to those humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many factors complicating the humanitarian aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll ask a more specific question. The question that you were being asked or a clause that was being asked of you on page 9255 at line 5 is that Mladic had imposed particular conditions upon the convoy being able to travel. Can you please tell the Court what conditions were being placed on the humanitarian aid to be received in the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That General Mladic wanted equivalent aid to be delivered to Bosnian Serb refugees to which General Morillon's and UNHCR's answer was that the statistics showed that the Bosnian Serbs were receiving as much if not more aid than the Bosnian Muslims. There were other factors as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to call up now 1D02-6111.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we see the conclusion of the letter, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: See who it's signed by. Yes, I think I recall this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And this letter was being addressed to both Mladic as well as Karadzic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to have a look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can move back to the first page, please. And if we move down just a bit further, there will also be the cc lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And at that time, you were indicating to Mladic and Karadzic in detail that the Bosnian Serbs were actually receiving more humanitarian aid than the Muslims; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get clear. We just saw the signatory to this letter, was it you? I didn't think it was your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was Mendiluce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I hear Madam Carter says you just indicated. Are you saying indicated in this letter, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he had actually responded previously in regards to my question about the humanitarian aid and the preconditions that were being placed upon it. And he had said that one of the conditions was that they wanted more aid to go to the Bosnian Serbs and that actually they had been receiving more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: More, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would have to get the specific line reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the issue is whether or not is Colonel Tucker who made the indication or whether or not it was the signatory of the letter, that would have been Mr. Mendiluce, and I believe it was Mr. Mendiluce who made the specific indication to Karadzic with the letter copied to Mladic with regard to where aid was going and what was the percentage of the that aid, and it's not the issue of you, the "you" is Mendiluce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm actually following up on the point that Colonel Tucker made in his own testimony today at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. But you see, when you do that after you've just put up a letter for us to look at, and we've just looked at who the signatory of the letter is, the impression you are giving us is that in this letter that's what is being indicated, and I would like you to separate the two if that is possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And while you do that, look at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm happy to take up this line after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After the break. Okay. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, still addressing 1D02-6111, the letter of Mendiluce in the opening paragraphs there's an indication that he is referring to a meeting that took place between General Mladic and General Morillon on 15 November, 1992. Is this the meeting that you were discussing with Mr. Guy-Smith yesterday in regards it to the humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He goes on to describe the preconditions that were being placed on these convoys. Are those the preconditions that were being set out to you in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware of UNHCR's response to these preconditions?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. And as the response is set out in this letter, you are familiar with those facts?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2695, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The final topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Why is it a D, sir? Oh P. P269 -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, as a final topic, I'd like to discuss with you the testimony from yesterday in regards to the Muslim prohibition of help into Sarajevo. I want to discuss that with you a bit further. Can you please tell me where did the gas line from heating run?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heating gas lines came from Russia through Serbia into Bosnia-Herzegovina and down into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And who turned off those gas lines?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the gas was either turned off in Serbia proper, or in Serb-held territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could just have clarification with regard to Serb-held territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that be Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb held territory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you also described in your previous testimony and you touched on it in yesterday's testimony about the Muslim populations who were responsible for, as was used by Judge Orie, the exploitation of misery. Who were these people who were trying to exploit the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have clear evidence as to named people. However, it was our conclusion that there were extremist radicals who would go to any lengths in order to try and achieve their objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was the Presidency's position in regards to the conditions of the Sarajevans?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency's position was that the position of their citizens in Sarajevo was unacceptable and was a disgrace and that all efforts should be made by the international community in order to ensure that the situation was improved, their citizens would no longer be under attack, and that they would be able to live safe lives free of fear, and with sufficient food, et cetera, to be able to live and survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I may have one moment to consult with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That completes my redirect. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I -- excuse me, Judge, my apologies but you are not getting interpreted. There's no interpretation on the screen. But also it indicates page 37, line 15, there's no interpretation. So your question is -- I'm rising in order so your question becomes part of the record, Your Honour, otherwise the question will be asked, but I don't think it will appear on the record, which I don't think is what you want to have occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat my question. Namely, that the international community in March of 1993 had a perception, had an impression that the Muslim population in the Srebrenica enclave will be a victim of the genocide, that genocide was being prepared at the time. Bearing in mind that situation, was this discussed, did they consider the possibility of evacuating the civilian population from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who came out with that possibility? Who discussed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs suggested it, and they created linkage between permitting people to be evacuated from Srebrenica, provided that Bosnian Serbs who were inside Tuzla would also be allowed to be evacuated out of the Bosnian Muslim held territory into Bosnian Serb held territory. That was one linkage. The second linkage was that the Bosnian Serbs nonetheless insisted on questioning every single male of combatant age who was evacuated -- who would be evacuated from Srebrenica in order to ascertain whether or not that person was a "war criminal" guilty of the massacres of Bosnian Serb villagers in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So their solution was discarded?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was partially attempted. The first attempt was the evacuation of Bosnian Serbs out of Tuzla which was one of the reasons that General Morillon went to Tuzla around the 19th, 20th of March. However, the Tuzla authorities with whom General Morillon met were very reluctant to permit this because they, from their perspective, they claimed that this would be paramount to them, the Bosnian Muslims, condoning ethnic cleansing, which was not something that they agreed with. Nonetheless, I believe that they allowed a small number of Bosnian Serbs, my recollection is something like 40, to leave Tuzla and go to Zvornik, and they did so in a convoy immediately after General Morillon when he left Tuzla. The second aspect is that on the convoy -- the humanitarian aid convoy which reached Srebrenica around the 26th of March, that convoy on its way out of Srebrenica took with it about 600 women and children and old men, who were then taken out through -- from Srebrenica to Zvornik, and I believe that the convoy then went on to Tuzla. I believe they discharged those people in Tuzla. However, there were no men on that convoy because they -- no men of combatant age. I was present when that convoy left, and I was present when the Serbs checked the convoy at the Yellow Bridge in order to check whether there were any men of combat. There was -- the next convoy in -- when it left there were - this is a matter of public record - there are television reports of hysterical people from Srebrenica desperately trying to climb onto these trucks in Srebrenica in order to be evacuated, and I believe that a number of people were squashed and killed in the rush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And following this first evacuation from Tuzla and Srebrenica, was there any more attempt?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were also, I believe, but again it's after I left, there were also further helicopter evacuations of injured of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand for the injured, but with regard to the civilian population in general, were there any more attempts?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was then after my time, and I would not be in a position to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why were there no longer any attempts?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I do not know whether there were or were not any further attempts. My last knowledge is of the hysterical behaviour which led to people being crushed. I do not know if there were any more attempts afterwards. I am not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, yesterday at page 10, line 9 to 12, you were asked by the Prosecution was the Srebrenica enclave being covered in international and local media. And your answer said, Yes, it was. Could you elaborate further on this point, make comments according to your experience of those days as to the extent and repercussions of this international and local coverage in the media.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- my understanding or my knowledge of the coverage, that is, I need to separate between Serb coverage, between Bosnian Muslim coverage, and international coverage. Bosnian -- sorry, Serb coverage on the day after that we arrived in Srebrenica was reporting that General Morillon and the UN team had been captured by the Bosnian Muslims and were being held hostage by the Bosnian Muslims and that Serb forces were attacking towards Srebrenica in order to rescue General Morillon. The local Bosnian Muslim, by this I mean "Oslobodenje," and local radio in the Tuzla area were reporting that there were continued attacks on the Srebrenica enclave and that -- people dying, that the United Nations had sent a team there and was trying to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid. The international community, there had been a big outcry in the international community about General Morillon's comments about after he came back from his visit to Cerska where he had said that he had not smelled the smell of burnt human flesh, and that was widely reported in the international media at the time. And when General Morillon went back into Tuzla on his second journey into -- on the way to Srebrenica, he was very angrily, verbally attacked by the commander of the Muslim forces in Tuzla and accused of all sorts of -- all sorts of things. And that was all in the international media. When we went into Srebrenica the second time -- went into Srebrenica for the first time, which was the second time into the enclave, there was a pause and then for about a day and a half and then the international media started reporting that General Morillon was in Srebrenica establishing what was going on. The major story which hit the international news was General Morillon's declaration that he made around the 13th/14th of March, which was referred to in testimony yesterday. And which -- at the end of which General Morillon declared that Srebrenica was under the protection of the United Nations. At that speech that General Morillon gave from the PTT building in Srebrenica, there were, as I said, a couple of journalists, and they immediately after that speech were permitted by the Srebrenica war committee to use the radio equipment in the PTT building in Srebrenica in order to speak with people in Sarajevo in order to file their dispatches about that story. And then there was a lot of international discussion back and forth about whether it was right or wrong or -- to be declaring a protected area, which has some -- there are some definitions about that and whether General Morillon was entitled to make such a statement. And the progress of discussions around the Srebrenica enclaves and attacks and fighting were daily reported in international media. I spoke by radio, by satellite radio, with my wife whilst I was in Srebrenica, and she told me that she had been reading about all these things in media from our home back in Germany. Does that answer your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench? Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: A single question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, were scenes from Srebrenica being broadcast on these television reports?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only later. And by "later" what I mean is the -- it was -- television was only brought into Srebrenica together with the later humanitarian aid convoys, and that is how the scenes from the hysterical refugees tried to clamber onto the trucks was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicated that there was Serb coverage, that you had been captured by Bosnian Muslims. I'm going to read something from your statement and see if that's what you are referring to. "On March 12th the situation changed completely. The crowd of refugees around the PTT building where we had spent the night had been growing and becoming increasingly hostile. As one stage, as I pushed my way through the with Mihailov, he told me the refugees were arguing amongst each other whether we should be killed immediately or whether we served any purpose in being kept alive. I also noticed a number of Bosniak soldiers setting up three heavy 12.7 mms," that's millimetre I guess? Thank you. "... millimetre machine-guns on tripods in positions to cover the road back the way we had come." Is that information that -- oh, I'm sorry, "... some more took up positions with hand-held anti-tank rockets." Is that information that you transmitted over any radio communication to anyone concerning your condition when you were telling us about you doing your hourly reporting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did report that information together with much other information over this HF radio that I've referred to. It was a UNHCR unencrypted radio, and we were aware that the Bosnian Serbs were certainly intercepting everything that we transmitted and sometimes jamming us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Colonel, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you so much for taking the time to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. Please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May I be excused from the remainder of the session so I may bid farewell to Colonel Tucker?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no more witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To what day do we adjourn? To Monday next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are waiting on some decisions of the Trial Chamber with respect to potential remaining witnesses. It is the Prosecution's projection that -- well, we are in the Chamber's hands. We are in the Chamber's hands because there are pending motions for three witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. The Chamber is working on those motions, and it will give its decision, but other than that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Other than that we do not have additional witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are then going to have to postpone sine die and the parties will be warned. Court adjourned.
